purpose: We already know that a covered call is when we buy 100 shares and sell a call against that same stock each week. The PMCC keeps the same weekly short, but instead of buying the 100 shares, we buy a ITM LEAP, which is a call with an expiry far away. In this case, we bought call that expires in Jan 2027, with 0.8 delta. Given this high delta it moves like 80 shares of stock, and since the strike is below that of the short call, it covers the short call. The main thing we are gaining here is cost, we are paying the instrinsict value of the LEAP, plus small amount of time value, we aren't paying the full share price. We can see that from day one, where the 100 shares cost $21279 vs the LEAP costs $5752, so we were able to buy the same weekly short call on basically one fourth of the capital. So is this initial saving worth what we had to give up?
expiry_rule:
Each Friday if the short call expires OTM, we keep the premium, or if it finishes ITM, in which case the rile buys it back at the intrinsic value, which is expiry close minus strike, at Friday's close. This is what we marked as an "assigned" week. Of the 26 calls sold, 20 expired and 6 were bought back, vv. So, we are buying back instead of accepting the assignment because in a PMCC, we don't own those 100 shares, so we wouldn't start short 100 Amazon shares on Monday vs a long call. To get flat we would need to buy shares, or exercise the LEAP early, which directly throws away its remaining time value. Closing the short call at expiry avoids both of these. And given that ITM call trades close to intrinsic value at expiry it as a realistic exit price.
So, the buyback ignores the bid/ask spread on expiry, and early assignment is not modeled. And Amazon pays no dividends, so early exercise of a call is unlikely
what_happened: So looking into more detail at what happened during this backtest, we can see the following: Over the window Apr to Oct, AMZN rose from $212.79 to $251.52, so up 18.2%, but most of this came in two seperate jumps, (April  and the June-July). The weekly calls behaved the way that covered calls usually do, 20 out of the 26 expired OTM, so we kept the premium, but the 6 that finished in the money cost more than all the 20 winners earned, so a net of -$1911 in both option books. Most of that loss came from the 2 jumps, when the stock blew throught the 30-delta in days. Because the short calls were identical, the book only differs in the long leg. THe 100 shares made $3873 and the LEAP $2672, because its delta was below 1 and lost time value over the six months. The PMCC also earned interest $249 on the cash it saved initially. So in summary, buy and hold made $3873, the covered call made $1923 and the PMCC made $1010
benefits:
So, where did the PMCC actually help? What it did was promise on the capital. IT ran the same 26 short calls with only $5752 tied up instead of $21279, this is 27% of the capital. In reality, instead of having this spare cash in T bills, we could use it do diversify the portfolio and take other positions. 
And per dollar commited it did better than the Covered Call, 13.2% against 9.2% for the covered call. 
In addition, the most we can lose is what we paid for the LEAP, (5k) vs for the shares its (21k), so in a creash the PMCC loses much fewer dollars. AMZN didn't actually fall enough in any moment during this period.
drawbacks: The PMCC main weakness we tested is that its losses are same size in dollars as the Covered call, buth they hit a much smaller amount of capital. So percentage wise it hurts much more. We saw this is the worst week (july 27), -2523 cost 44% of the $5752, vs 12% of the covered calls $21279. So the initial capital savings are leverage, and this leverage works in both directions. The long leg also gave up return, LEAP only made 69% vs the sahres, because of the below 1 delta, and it losing time value over the 6 months. In terms of Sharpe ratio, it comes the worst of the 3.
verdict: My opinion, would be not to deploy. Because it did not earn more even if we had started with the same capital, and it earns less per unit of risk than the covered call. We must consider though, that this rising market is a bad regime for this call-selling strategy. So these results reflect the regime more than they do the actual trading strategy. With a different regime, the option books could have beat the buy and hold. Something else that is important, is where we could invest the capital saved, and consider why we could want a strategy that requires less initial capital.
